subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 7 periods = 350 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 50min

textbook_items_in_class.description: Pens-and-pencils scenario introducing terms, variables, coefficients, and constant in the expression 4x + 5y + 3.
Wire bent into a rectangle; area expressed as the one-variable expression x(10-x) = 10x - x^2.
Find the degrees of four given polynomials.
Find the coefficients of x^2 and x^3 in a given degree-4 polynomial.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pens-and-pencils scenario (Example 1, p.16): write the expression 4x + 5y + 3 on the board and ask students to identify each term, name the variables, and state the coefficient of each variable term and the constant. Then present Example 3, p.17 — the wire-into-rectangle scenario — and guide students to form x(10-x) = 10x - x^2, noticing how a single variable can produce different powers.

From the two examples, draw out the definition of a univariate polynomial: one variable, whole-number exponents, finite terms. On the board, list the expressions encountered and ask students to identify the highest power in each — establishing degree. Name the four types: linear (degree 1), quadratic (degree 2), cubic (degree 3), and constant (degree 0), placing each example from the board into its category. Pause for the Think and Reflect prompt from this section: students examine several given algebraic expressions, compare them for similarities and differences, and identify terms, variables, and coefficients in pairs before sharing.

Students individually attempt Exercise Set 2.1 Q1, p.18 (find degrees of four polynomials) and Q3, p.18 (find coefficients of x^2 and x^3 in a degree-4 polynomial). Circulate and check for the common slip of confusing the degree of a term with its coefficient.

Brief whole-class consolidation: call on two students to share their answers to Q1 and Q3, address any disagreements on the board, and close by asking the class to state — without looking at notes — the degree and type of the polynomial 7x^3 - 2x + 5.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's vocabulary work: ensure students distinguish coefficient (the multiplier of a variable term) from the constant term, and degree (the highest power) from the number of terms — these two confusions appear consistently on Q3 and E-4. Example 2, p.16-17 (the two-variable garden scenario) is a well-structured self-study read for students who finish early or want a richer context.
homework: Exercise Set 2.1 Q2, p.18 — write polynomials of degrees 1, 2, and 3, choosing your own coefficients and justifying which is which.

periods.activity_title: Defining Linear Polynomials and Solving Linear Equations

textbook_items_in_class.description: Perimeter of a square of side x as the linear polynomial 4x.
Chess club joining fee plus per-match charge modelled as the linear polynomial 200 + 50m.
Sum-of-two-numbers word problem solved via the linear equation 2x + 10 = 64; also introduces evaluating a linear expression as an input-output process.
Evaluate the linear polynomial 5x-3 at three given values of x (sub-parts i-iii).
Find present ages of Salil and his mother from a linear-equation age relationship.
Find the dimensions of a rectangle given its perimeter and a relation between length and width.

time_bands.activity: Present Example 4, p.19 (perimeter of a square) and Example 5, p.19 (chess-club fees). Ask: what is common to 4x and 200 + 50m? Guide students to observe: one variable, highest power 1, constant and linear term. Formally define a linear polynomial as ax + b with a ≠ 0, and note the constant (degree 0) as the limiting case. Establish that successive integer values of a linear polynomial always differ by the same amount — the constant a — linking to what will come in Section 2.3.

Work through Example 6, p.20 with the class: translate the word problem into the equation 2x + 10 = 64, solve step by step, and verify the answer by substituting back. Use this to define equating a linear polynomial to a constant as a linear equation and to frame the polynomial as an input-output function — a given input x produces a definite output. Introduce the Think and Reflect prompt: students compute a linear polynomial at a specified value, then work backward — given the output, find the input — before comparing approaches.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 2.2 Q1, p.21 (evaluate 5x - 3 at three values), Q3, p.21 (age problem — form and solve a linear equation), and Q7, p.21 (rectangle dimensions from perimeter). Circulate; watch for sign errors when rearranging the equation and for students who evaluate correctly but set up the word-problem equation incorrectly.

Full-class debrief of Q3 and Q7: ask one student to write their equation on the board and another to verify the solution by substitution. Highlight how the same solve-and-verify process works across different word-problem contexts.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established what a polynomial is and what its degree means, this unit narrows to the linear case and introduces the solving step. A frequent error is forming the equation correctly but then dividing both sides by the variable rather than the coefficient — reinforce that only numbers move across the equality, not the variable. Exercise Set 2.2 Q5, p.21 (coins problem) and Q6, p.21 (fence pieces) are solid self-study items for students who complete classwork early.
homework: Exercise Set 2.2 Q4, p.21 and Q5, p.21 — set up and solve linear equations for each, writing one sentence explaining what the variable represents.

periods.activity_title: Generalising Linear Patterns from Geometric and Real-World Sequences

textbook_items_in_class.description: Bela's pocket money depletion modelled as 100 - 5n, solved for the day the amount left equals 40.
Auto-rickshaw fare with flat initial charge plus per-km rate, modelled as 15n - 5 for n >= 2.
Find a linear expression for a savings account balance growing by a fixed monthly amount.
Express remaining pages of a book read at a constant daily rate as a linear pattern.

time_bands.activity: Open with the growing-square-tiles pattern from the section: draw stage 1, 2, 3 on the board (1, 3, 5 tiles) and ask students to predict stage 4 and stage 10, writing down their reasoning. Record differences between consecutive terms and ask: what is always constant? Through class discussion, generalise to the nth term: 2n - 1. Define a linear pattern as a sequence with constant difference between consecutive terms, and note this is precisely the behaviour of a linear polynomial evaluated at successive integers.

Present the Think and Reflect prompt: students evaluate the expression 2n - 1 at a large n (say n = 50), then reverse — given the value 99, find n. Then work through Example 7, p.22-23 (Bela's pocket money 100 - 5n) and Example 8, p.23 (auto-rickshaw fare 15n - 5) together, emphasising the step of identifying the constant difference and building the expression before solving.

Students work in pairs on Exercise Set 2.3 Q1, p.23 (savings growing by a fixed monthly amount — build the expression and evaluate) and Q5, p.24 (book-reading depletion — express remaining pages and find when the book is finished). Pairs share their expressions with a neighbouring pair and check each other's constant-difference reasoning.

Whole-class close: ask a pair to present the expression for Q5 and justify why it is linear. Ask the class: what changes in the expression when the book is thicker but the reading rate is the same? This surfaces the structural difference between the constant term and the coefficient.

periods.teacher_notes: Having seen linear polynomials evaluated at specific inputs, students now derive them from a pattern's structure — the constant difference is the coefficient of n and the stage-0 intercept is the constant term. A recurring slip is writing the nth-term expression with the wrong sign on the constant (e.g., writing 5n - 100 instead of 100 - 5n for a depleting quantity); the table of values is the fastest diagnostic. Exercise Set 2.3 Q3, p.24 (rectangle areas) and Q4, p.24 (box volumes) extend the pattern idea into two-variable contexts and are good self-study for confident students.
homework: Exercise Set 2.3 Q2, p.24 — write the linear expression for rally membership decreasing by a fixed amount each hour, then find how many hours until the membership reaches a specified value.

periods.activity_title: Linear Growth and Linear Decay: Modelling and Distinguishing

textbook_items_in_class.description: Journey cost function C(d) = 100 + 60d illustrating linear growth via a table of values.
Water height in a tank h(t) = 3 - 0.5t illustrating linear decay via a table of values.
Model plant height growing at a constant monthly rate; find height after 7 months, tabulate, and justify linear growth (sub-parts i-iii).
Model a depreciating mobile phone value; find value after 3 years, tabulate, and justify linear decay (sub-parts i-iii).

time_bands.activity: Present Example 9, p.24 (C(d) = 100 + 60d) and Example 10, p.24-25 (h(t) = 3 - 0.5t) side by side on the board. For each, build a small table of values (d or t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4) and ask students to state the change from row to row. Label the first as linear growth (constant positive increase) and the second as linear decay (constant negative decrease), writing down a precise definition of each.

Address the Think and Reflect prompt from this section: given a new scenario (e.g., a candle burning down at a fixed rate), students extend the function to a new input, identify whether it is growth or decay, and justify in one sentence. Collect two or three answers and discuss what in the expression's structure (sign of the coefficient of the input variable) determines the classification.

Students work individually on Exercise Set 2.4 Q1, p.25 (plant height — model, evaluate at 7 months, tabulate, justify) and Q2, p.25 (phone depreciation — model, evaluate at 3 years, tabulate, justify). For each, require students to write the expression first, then the table, then one sentence of justification naming the constant change per interval.

Pair-share: each student compares their Q1 and Q2 expressions with a partner, checking whether the sign of the coefficient of the time variable correctly reflects growth or decay. Close by asking: can the same expression represent both growth and decay depending on context? Discuss briefly.

periods.teacher_notes: Having built linear expressions from patterns and word problems, students now name the two functional behaviours — growth and decay — and anchor them to the sign of the coefficient. The most common confusion is calling a function 'linear growth' whenever the expression has a positive constant term, regardless of the coefficient's sign; reinforce that it is the rate (the coefficient of the input variable) that determines growth or decay. Exercise Set 2.4 Q3, p.25-26 and Q4, p.26 are good self-study for students who finish early — both require writing, evaluating, and justifying in sub-parts.
homework: Exercise Set 2.4 Q4, p.26 — write the linear equation for the depleting prepaid balance, find when it runs out, and complete the table of values with sub-parts i-iii.

periods.activity_title: Deriving a Linear Relationship y = ax + b from Two Data Points

textbook_items_in_class.description: Telecom data-billing scenario; finds a and b in y = ax + b from two given (x, y) pairs by solving simultaneous equations.
Find a and b in a learning-platform billing relation y = ax+b from two given module-count/bill pairs.
Find a and b in a gym court-rental billing relation y = ax+b from two given hour/bill pairs.
Find a and b in the Celsius-Fahrenheit linear relation from the freezing and boiling reference points.

time_bands.activity: Present Example 11, p.25-26 in full: pose the two given data points, write the two equations by substituting each pair into y = ax + b, subtract to eliminate b and find a, then substitute back to find b. Work each algebraic step slowly on the board, narrating the simultaneous-equations method. Verify by substituting both original pairs back into the derived equation.

Address the Think and Reflect prompt: once a and b are found, students interpret their real-world meaning — a is the per-unit rate (cost per gigabyte), b is the fixed charge. Collect interpretations and build a sentence frame on the board: 'a represents ___ per ___ and b represents the fixed ___.' Discuss whether b can be negative in some real-world contexts.

Students work individually through Exercise Set 2.5 Q1, p.27 (learning-platform billing), Q2, p.27 (court-rental), and Q3, p.27 (Celsius-Fahrenheit). For Q3, note that the two reference points are given as known scientific facts; students substitute these into y = ax + b and solve. Circulate and watch for errors in the subtraction step when eliminating b, especially where the two x-values are not simple integers.

Quick whole-class check: ask for the values of a and b in Q3 and verify the freezing point (0°C = 32°F) and boiling point (100°C = 212°F) hold. Highlight that the verification step — substituting the original data back — applies to every problem of this type.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with linear expressions evaluated at known inputs, this unit reverses the direction: two outputs are known and students recover the parameters. The typical algebraic slip is subtracting the two equations incorrectly when the x-values require scaling before subtraction; reinforce the subtraction step explicitly. Example 11, p.25-26 is the chapter's only fully worked illustration of this method, so students who find Q3 difficult should re-read it as a self-study reference before attempting the Celsius problem again.

periods.activity_title: Plotting Linear Equations and Reading Slope and Intercept from Graphs
periods.visual_aids: Coordinate axes on the board with y = 3x plotted (Example 12, p.28-29) and y = (1/2)x, y = x, y = 2x on shared axes (Example 14, p.29-31)

textbook_items_in_class.description: Plots five points and identifies the line y = 3x by observing the constant ratio between coordinates.
Graphs y = (1/2)x, y = x, y = 2x together to compare slope steepness as a varies for a > 0.
Graphs y = 2x-1, y = 2x+1, y = 2x+5 individually and together, and y = x+3, y = 2x+5, y = 3x-2 together, to establish slope and y-intercept and the parallel-lines property.

time_bands.activity: On pre-drawn axes, reproduce Example 12, p.28-29: list five (x, y) pairs satisfying y = 3x, plot them, and draw the line. Ask students: where does the line cross the y-axis? What is the ratio y/x at every plotted point? Establish that for y = ax + b, the line crosses the y-axis at (0, b) — the y-intercept — and that a governs steepness.

Work through Example 14, p.29-31 on the board: plot y = (1/2)x, y = x, and y = 2x on shared axes, labelling each. Ask students to state which line is steepest and why. Introduce the definition of slope a formally: the constant rise per unit run. Address the Think and Reflect prompt from Section 2.6: students identify one additional point on each plotted line and predict what the graph of y = 4x would look like before the teacher draws it.

Walk through Example 16, p.33-36 step by step: first plot y = 2x - 1, y = 2x + 1, y = 2x + 5 and ask students to state what is common (same slope, different intercepts — parallel lines). Then overlay y = x + 3, y = 2x + 5, y = 3x - 2 to show how varying a while fixing different b values changes steepness. Students sketch both families on their own graph paper.

Students answer the Think and Reflect prompt extension in writing: compare the graphs of two lines with slopes of opposite signs, describing the difference in appearance. Collect responses to gauge readiness for the consolidation unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The key deductive move here is deriving the roles of a and b from the general form y = ax + b and reading them off plotted lines — not discovering them afresh. A common confusion is thinking that a larger positive b (higher y-intercept) means a steeper line; reinforce that steepness is controlled by a alone. Example 13, p.29 (negative slope, five points) and Example 15, p.31-33 (comparing negative slopes) are natural self-study companions for students who want to extend their graph-comparison work.
homework: Exercise Set 2.6 Q1, p.36 — draw the five sets of lines (sub-parts i-v) on graph paper and write one sentence for each set stating what role a and b play.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Slope, Intercept, and Growth/Decay Across Linear Graphs
periods.visual_aids: Coordinate axes on board showing y = -(1/3)x, y = -x, y = -3x on shared axes (Example 15, p.31-33)

textbook_items_in_class.description: Plots five points and identifies the line through them (negative slope case).
Graphs y = -(1/3)x, y = -x, y = -3x together to compare slope steepness as a varies for negative slopes.
Draw five sets of lines (sub-parts i-v) and reflect on the role of slope a and y-intercept b in each set.

time_bands.activity: Open with Example 13, p.29 (negative-slope line): students plot the five given points on their graph paper and identify the line, noting that the slope is negative — the line falls left to right. Then display Example 15, p.31-33 on the board: y = -(1/3)x, y = -x, y = -3x on shared axes. Students state which is steepest and connect this to the magnitude of a, reinforcing that sign determines direction and magnitude determines steepness.

Address the Think and Reflect prompt: students compare two lines with slopes of opposite signs (one from the positive family of Unit 6, one from the negative family here) drawn on the same axes, and state in writing how they differ in appearance and what that means for the growth/decay classification. Discuss two or three responses and formalise: a > 0 gives linear growth (rising line), a < 0 gives linear decay (falling line).

Students work on Exercise Set 2.6 Q1, p.36 (any sub-parts not yet completed): draw the assigned families of lines on graph paper and write one sentence per sub-part explaining the role of a and b in that family. Circulate and check that students are plotting at least two points per line before drawing, and that parallel lines in a family are correctly identified as sharing the same slope.

Whole-class close: pose the question — 'A line passes through (0, 4) and (2, 10). What are its slope a and y-intercept b?' Students solve individually (a = 3, b = 4), then a volunteer writes the working on the board. This ties the graphical interpretation of a and b back to the simultaneous-equations method of Section 2.5, completing the chapter's conceptual arc.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit completes the graphical strand by handling negative slopes and consolidating the link between the sign of a and growth or decay. Students sometimes confuse a steeper negative slope (e.g., -3) with a 'bigger' (less negative) quantity, reversing the ordering; comparing |a| values explicitly on the board helps. The closing problem — finding a and b from two plotted points — deliberately recalls the algebraic method of Section 2.5, so students who need a reminder can self-check against Example 11, p.25-26.

questions.question_text: The polynomial 5x³ − 7x² + 2x − 9 has degree 3. Which of the following correctly states both its type and the coefficient of x²?

options.label: A
options.text: Cubic polynomial; coefficient of x² is 2

options.label: B
options.text: Cubic polynomial; coefficient of x² is 7

options.label: C
options.text: Cubic polynomial; coefficient of x² is −7

options.label: D
options.text: Quadratic polynomial; coefficient of x² is −7

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student identifies the type correctly but drops the negative sign on the coefficient, confusing the coefficient with its absolute value.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student reads the highest-degree term present as x² rather than x³, misidentifying the degree and therefore the type.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student locates the coefficient of x (the linear term) instead of x², confusing which term is being asked about.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who struggles with multi-part recall can first circle only the x² term and state its multiplier before classifying the type. A student ready for challenge can write a new degree-4 polynomial with a specified coefficient of x³ and explain why it is not cubic.

questions.question_text: A school sports club charges a registration fee of ₹150 plus ₹40 for each match a student plays. A student paid a total of ₹390. Write a linear equation to model this situation and solve it to find the number of matches the student played. Verify your answer by substituting it back into your equation.
questions.method_one_line: Set 150 + 40m = 390, subtract 150 from both sides to get 40m = 240, then divide by 40 to get m = 6; verify: 150 + 40(6) = 150 + 240 = 390 ✓.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who finds the equation setup difficult can begin by building a table of total cost for 1, 2, 3… matches until reaching 390. A student ready for extension can be asked: for what number of matches would two students — one on this plan and one paying ₹50 per match with no registration fee — pay the same total?

questions.question_text: The polynomial P(x) = 8x − 5 models the output of a process for a whole-number input x. (i) Find P(4) and P(7). (ii) For which value of x does P(x) = 67? Show all working.
questions.method_one_line: For (i) substitute x = 4 and x = 7 directly; for (ii) set 8x − 5 = 67, add 5 to both sides: 8x = 72, divide by 8: x = 9; verify: 8(9) − 5 = 72 − 5 = 67 ✓.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain about the reverse step can build a short input-output table for x = 1 through 10 and locate the row where the output is 67 before writing the equation. A student seeking a challenge can be asked to find all integer inputs for which P(x) is divisible by 5.

questions.question_text: Refer to the table provided. (i) State the constant difference and write a linear expression for the number of stickers at stage n. (ii) Find the number of stickers at stage 20. (iii) At which stage does the number of stickers equal 64? Show all working.
questions.method_one_line: Find the constant difference between consecutive terms, express as 3n + b, substitute n = 1 and term = 4 to find b = 1; evaluate at n = 20; set equal to 64 and solve.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who struggles to form the general expression can first extend the table to stage 5 and 6, confirm the constant difference, and then use the form 'starting value + (n−1) × difference' as a scaffold before simplifying. A student ready for extension can be asked to find the first stage at which the sticker count exceeds 100.

questions.question_text: A streetlight dimmer reduces a bulb's brightness by 8 lumens every minute after it is switched on. The starting brightness is 200 lumens. (i) Write a linear expression B(t) for the brightness after t minutes. (ii) Find B(15). (iii) State whether this is linear growth or linear decay and justify your answer by referring to the coefficient of t in your expression.
expected_elements: Justification naming the coefficient of t as −8 (negative), indicating a constant decrease per unit time

SCR.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain can build a table of B(t) for t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 first, observe the constant decrease of 8, and then write the expression. A student ready for a challenge can be asked to find the time at which the bulb reaches 0 lumens and explain why B(t) is not physically meaningful for larger t.

competency.competency_text: Model real-world situations as linear expressions or equations and solve them to draw conclusions.

questions.question_text: A parking facility charges customers according to the linear relationship C = ax + b, where x is the number of hours parked and C is the total charge in rupees. Parking for 2 hours costs ₹70 and parking for 5 hours costs ₹130. (i) Set up two simultaneous equations in a and b and solve them to find a and b. (ii) Write the complete linear relationship. (iii) Explain in one sentence what a and b each represent in the context of this parking facility. (iv) A customer is charged ₹190. How many hours did they park? Show your working and verify your answer.
look_for: Correct formation of the two equations: 2a + b = 70 and 5a + b = 130
Correct subtraction step to eliminate b: 3a = 60, so a = 20
Contextual interpretation: a = 20 is the charge per hour; b = 30 is the fixed entry/base charge

ECR.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain about the simultaneous-equations step can substitute both given (x, C) pairs into C = ax + b one at a time, write the resulting numerical equations, and then reason about what must be subtracted to isolate a. A student ready for extension can be asked whether two data points always uniquely determine a linear relationship and when this might fail.

questions.question_text: On graph paper, plot the line y = 2x + 3 by computing and marking exactly two points, then drawing the line through them. (i) State the y-intercept and slope of the line directly from the equation. (ii) Mark the y-intercept on your graph and confirm it matches your computed point. (iii) A second line is given by y = 2x − 5. Without plotting, state whether this line is parallel to y = 2x + 3, steeper, or less steep, and justify your answer using the values of a and b.
questions.expected_answer: y-intercept = 3 (at (0,3)); slope = 2. Second line y = 2x − 5 has slope 2 and y-intercept −5; same slope as y = 2x + 3, so the lines are parallel (not steeper or less steep).
questions.method_one_line: Read a = 2 and b = 3 directly from y = ax + b; plot (0, 3) and one other point found by substitution; for the second line, compare slopes: both a = 2 means parallel lines.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain about reading a and b from the equation can substitute x = 0 and x = 1 to generate two explicit points and then state the y-intercept as the point where x = 0. A student ready for extension can be asked to sketch a third line through (0, 3) with slope 4 on the same axes and explain why it is not parallel to the first two lines.

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can compare families of linear graphs to determine how varying a (with b fixed) or varying b (with a fixed) changes the line, and distinguish positive-slope from negative-slope graphs.
questions.section_context: Graphing y = ax + b: plotting, slope steepness, y-intercept, parallel lines, growth vs decay

questions.question_text: Three lines are given: L₁: y = 3x + 2, L₂: y = −3x + 2, L₃: y = (1/2)x + 2. (i) Without plotting, compare the steepness of L₁ and L₃ and explain which is steeper and why. (ii) Compare the graphs of L₁ and L₂. They share the same y-intercept — in what way do their graphs differ, and what does the sign of the slope tell you about the behaviour of each? (iii) Explain why L₁ and L₂ are not parallel to each other, even though they have the same value of |a|. Use the definition of slope to justify your answer.
look_for: Correct comparison of L₁ and L₃: |a| = 3 > 1/2, so L₁ is steeper; reasoning explicitly uses the magnitude of a as the measure of steepness
Correct description of L₁ vs L₂: both cross the y-axis at (0, 2), but L₁ rises left to right (positive slope, linear growth) while L₂ falls left to right (negative slope, linear decay)
Correct explanation that L₁ and L₂ are not parallel because they have different slopes (a = 3 and a = −3 are not equal), and the definition that parallel lines share the same slope
No confusion between |a| equal meaning the slopes are equal — the sign is part of the slope value, not separate from it

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds the purely symbolic comparison difficult can sketch rough graphs of L₁ and L₃ — plotting (0,2) and one other point for each — before reasoning about steepness. A student ready for extension can be asked to construct a fourth line L₄ parallel to L₂ but passing through (0, −1) and write its equation.
